summary.text: An ocean gyre is a large system of surface currents that moves in a circle, driven by the wind.
The largest gyres are controlled by global wind belts: easterlies in the tropics and westerlies in the midlatitudes.
A gyre's return flow is squeezed into a western boundary current much stronger than its interior flow, an effect called western intensification.

facts.label: Currents per gyre
facts.value: Typically four in a subtropical gyre

facts.label: North Atlantic center
facts.value: The Sargasso Sea, thick with Sargassum seaweed

items.prompt: Seen from above, which way does a subtropical gyre in the southern hemisphere turn?
items.explain: Because of the Coriolis force, subtropical gyres turn clockwise in the northern hemisphere and counterclockwise in the southern.

items.prompt: A gyre's return flow must carry as much water as its wide interior, but through a far narrower strip on the western side. What does that mean for the current in that strip?

options.label: It is weaker and slower than the interior
It is much stronger than the interior
It flows the same way as the interior

items.explain: Moving the same amount of water through a much smaller area makes western boundary currents much stronger, called western intensification.

items.prompt: In the middle of the North Atlantic Gyre lies a sea named after something that gathers there in thick mats. What is it?
items.explain: The gyre's center is the Sargasso Sea, known for its dense build-up of Sargassum seaweed.

items.prompt: What sets the largest ocean gyres in motion and decides where they sit?

options.label: The daily pull of the tides

items.explain: The largest gyres are wind-driven: prevailing winds control both where they are and how they move.

items.prompt: Africa does not reach as far south as the Indian Ocean Gyre. What does this let some water in the Agulhas Current do?

options.label: Drain north into the Red Sea

items.explain: With no land in the way, some Agulhas water leaks into the Atlantic Ocean.

items.prompt: Winds over a subtropical gyre drive Ekman pumping, which pushes water downward. How does the sea surface at the gyre's center compare with its surroundings?

options.label: It sits in a shallow dip
It swings up and down daily

items.explain: Ekman pumping in subtropical gyres raises the sea surface height at the gyre's center.

paragraphs.heading: A wheel of currents
paragraphs.text: An ocean gyre is a huge system of surface currents that turns in a circle, pushed along by the wind. The word can mean any swirl in the air or the sea, even one that people make. Most often, though, oceanographers use it for the great current systems of the world's oceans.

paragraphs.heading: Set in motion by wind belts
paragraphs.text: The biggest gyres are wind-driven, so the planet's steady wind belts decide where they sit and how they behave: easterlies in the tropics and westerlies in the middle latitudes. The Coriolis effect is what makes them form. The twisting force of the wind on the water, called the wind stress curl, pushes water down in the subtropics, a process named Ekman pumping. In the subpolar regions it draws water up instead, which is called Ekman suction.

paragraphs.heading: Hills and dips in the sea
paragraphs.text: These vertical motions change the height of the sea itself. Ekman pumping raises the sea surface at the middle of a subtropical gyre, and the currents around it turn in the anticyclonic direction. Ekman suction lowers the sea surface in a subpolar gyre, where the currents turn the cyclonic way.

paragraphs.heading: Why the west side runs fast
paragraphs.text: Across most of their area, subtropical gyres drift slowly toward the equator and subpolar gyres drift slowly toward the pole, as the Sverdrup balance describes. Water has to come back the other way to keep mass in balance, and the Sverdrup solution could not say how. Henry Stommel and Walter Munk showed that the return flow is squeezed into a strong current along the western edge. The same holds for every gyre in both hemispheres. Because this western boundary current carries about as much water as the whole slow interior, but through a far narrower space, it is much stronger, an effect called western intensification.

paragraphs.heading: The five big gyres
paragraphs.text: The world has five major subtropical gyres: the North Atlantic, South Atlantic, Indian Ocean, North Pacific and South Pacific gyres. All of them are anticyclonic, which means they turn clockwise north of the equator and counterclockwise south of it, a result of the Coriolis force. A typical one is built from four currents: a westward current near the equator, a narrow, strong current running poleward on the western side, an eastward current in the middle latitudes, and a broader, weaker current returning toward the equator on the eastern side.

paragraphs.heading: Around the North Atlantic
paragraphs.text: The North Atlantic Gyre shows the pattern. The North Equatorial Current carries warm water west to the Caribbean, where it meets the warm water of the Gulf of Mexico and becomes the Gulf Stream, a western boundary current. That flow heads north and east toward Europe as the North Atlantic Current. The Canary Current then runs south past Europe and north Africa to close the loop. In the middle lies the Sargasso Sea, known for its dense build-up of Sargassum seaweed.

paragraphs.heading: A leak at Africa's tip
paragraphs.text: In the Indian Ocean Gyre, the South Equatorial Current flows west toward Africa, and Madagascar splits it into the Mozambique Current and the East Madagascar Current. South of the island the two join as the Agulhas Current, which runs south to meet the eastward Antarctic Circumpolar Current. Africa does not reach as far south as the gyre does, so some Agulhas water spills into the Atlantic. That leak may matter for the global thermohaline circulation.
